transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
U.S. officials are trying to calm public health fears over controlled detonation tomorrow morning
in Iowa.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports the Army and multiple agencies have held a public briefing
about the plan to destroy an explosive stockpile in Middletown.
The possible toxic fallout from detonating a stockpile of unstable explosives has raised
concerns for people and livestock, some of whom have been advised to evacuate.
At the briefing, Army Major General Eric Shirley said the ordinance could explode spontaneously
if it's not destroyed now.
We know and are confident and have the full concurrence of all the agencies who have been
participating in this, that the controlled detonation is absolutely the only way to go.
This comes after days of confusion and President Trump saying he would blame the incoming Democratic
Governor-elect of Iowa for any harm if the explosion were delayed.
The Army has been aware of the danger since March and later discarded a plan to use chemicals
to neutralize the stockpile.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
President Trump, investors and some employees are cheering Jensen Wong's return as CEO
of NVIDIA.
But not everyone is policed, and PR's Andrea Shee reports Wong's critics include those
who've worked to change Silicon Valley's tech bro culture.
Unfathomable. A backslide.
Those are words that some are using to describe the decision by NVIDIA's board to reinstate
Wong after finding him in violation of the company's code of conduct.
Frieda Caper Klein has long used her role as an investor to promote diversity and inclusion
in Silicon Valley.
She says Wong's swift comeback sends a troubling message.
You can violate corporate policy.
You can possibly threaten national security.
You can make up your own rules as you go, as long as you bring in the money.
Videos posted to social media show Wong arriving at company headquarters to loud applause.
He tells the crowd he'll be a better CEO the second time around.
Andrea Shee, NPR News.
New research shows people taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss may also see higher breast
density and subsequent mammograms.
Here's NPR's Yuki Noguchi.
The study being presented at the Radiological Society of America looked back at 107 women,
age 39 to 79, who had gotten mammograms before and after starting a regimen of GLP-1 drugs
like Wagovia or ZEPFOUND.
Breast density increased for 62.5 percent of women.
Normally, dense breasts are associated with higher breast cancer risk, in part because
the fibroglangellar tissue can obscure tumors.
But in this case, researchers are not yet certain that the tissue composition of the
breast or the cancer risk changes with GLP-1 use.
The researchers advise people taking the drugs to continue routine breast cancer screening
as recommended.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Medicare unveiled its latest round of discounted drug prices for beneficiaries.
The lower prices for 13 drugs will take effect in January of 2028.
NPR's Sydney Lupkin has more.
Medicare says it negotiated an 84 percent discount on Eli Lilly's popular type 2 diabetes
drug Trulicity.
That puts it at $150 a month.
Trulicity is an older GLP-1 drug, and unlike Lilly's ZEPFOUND, it's not approved for weight
loss.
But the Medicare price for Trulicity is lower than the $245 the White House negotiated for
newer GLP-1s, including Ozempic.
Medicare also negotiated discounts for drugs that treat HIV, various cancers, and inflammatory
conditions like Crohn's disease.
This is the third round of Medicare drug price negotiations and the first to include intravenous
drugs covered by Medicare Part B. Overall, the program has negotiated the prices of 37
drugs since it started in August of 2023.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
As Thanksgiving week travel ramps up, parts of the West Coast are bracing for Pacific
Coast king tides that could break records set more than 40 years ago.
The National Weather Service says the biggest tides of the year could hit 2.8 feet above
normal in the San Francisco Bay area.
Low-lying shores from California to Washington State face flood risks.
Gunmen are holding two dozen people hostage at a supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia.
Local media reported an attempted robbery escalated into the hostage situation and prompted
a massive police response.
Last night in Villa Vicencio, a car bomb exploded, injuring at least 23 people.
The president of Colombia blamed narco-terrorism for that attack.
It's NPR.
This week on NPR's Up First, NVIDIA's CEO is back on the job.
What does that mean for your wallet?
The Thanksgiving travel rush begins in the aftermath of airline and FAA meltdowns.
What does that mean for your plans?
Also the holiday shopping season is underway.
It's a lot to track during the busy time of the year, so make our short daily episodes
a part of your morning routine.
Listen every weekday to Up First from NPR News.

topics.text: Army plans controlled detonation of unstable explosives stockpile in Middletown, Iowa, drawing public health fears
NVIDIA board reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after code of conduct violation, drawing criticism from investors
Study finds breast density increases in most women taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, researchers unsure of cancer risk
Medicare announces negotiated discounted prices for 13 drugs, including Eli Lilly's Trulicity at $150 monthly
Pacific Coast king tides forecast to break 40-year records, raising flood risks from California to Washington
Gunmen take two dozen hostage at supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia after attempted robbery
Car bomb explodes in Villa Vicencio, Colombia, injuring at least 23 people
